title: Regular Expression Multiline Anchors Trap
platform_conditions: Ruby 3.x standard library; ^ and $ are line anchors in Ruby regex, and Regexp.timeout exists only from Ruby 3.2+
security_mechanism: In Ruby, ^ and $ anchor to line boundaries, so a validator like /^https:\/\/example\.com$/ accepts 'https://example.com.attacker.tld\narbitrary' or any payload where the wanted prefix appears at a line start and everything else sits after a newline; \A and \z anchor the actual string boundaries ($ additionally matches before a trailing newline, \Z does too, only \z does not). The same unchecked-input shape feeds catastrophic backtracking: nested quantifiers over overlapping alternations drive exponential CPU on one thread, and only Ruby 3.2's Regexp.timeout bounds it. Converting external input with to_sym feeds attacker-chosen symbols into method and lookup namespaces; since Ruby 2.2 symbols are garbage-collected, so the historical memory-exhaustion angle is bounded, but the lookup-collision angle remains.

source_sink_clues.source: URLs, identifiers and multiline strings supplied by clients and validated with anchored regexes; patterns and subjects driving backtracking.
source_sink_clues.sink: =~ / match on security gates using ^...$ or $-anchored patterns; Regexp.new with input-derived patterns; to_sym on external input used for lookups

tracking_guards: Require \A / \z anchors (not ^ / $) in validators, plus explicit rejection of \n in the validated value; require Regexp.timeout (Ruby 3.2+) or bounded input length with constant patterns; require to_sym inputs to come from a fixed set.
not_candidate_when: The pattern is anchored with \A/\z and newlines are rejected explicitly, the regex is a constant without nested quantifiers and the subject is length-bounded, or to_sym operates on values drawn from a server-side fixed set.
